newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey secularists rally round half-chance Yilmaz.
newsitem.headline: Turkey secularists rally round half-chance Yilmaz.

text.p: Turkey's secularists have a new champion in conservative prime minister-designate Mesut Yilmaz, but their dream of banishing the Islamists from political life may prove as elusive as ever.

In fact, the biggest loser could well be Yilmaz's rival rightist leader Tansu Ciller, whose position as darling of the media and toast of Western capitals was undermined by her decision one year ago to join an Islamist-led coalition.

Mainstream newspapers gloated at the weekend over the decision by President Suleyman Demirel to reject a delicate power-sharing deal that would have kept the Islam-based Welfare Party in the ruling coalition under Ciller's stewardship.

Instead, Demirel used his constitutional powers to hand the mandate to the pro-Western Yilmaz, who has pledged to forge an "Islamist-free" coalition by June 30 from among the country's fractious political factions.
"(Demirel) ends the Welfare-Path," taunted the mass-circulation Sabah daily, using the former coalition's nickname. "A Shock for Welfare-Path," said rival Hurriyet.
That shuts the door, at least for now, on outgoing Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan, who was forced by army pressure to resign last week as modern Turkey's first Islamist leader.
Political commentator Cengiz Candar said any Yilmaz-led alliance would represent "a state government" -- that is, free of any Islamist taint.
"This means the kind of government that high-ranking commanders of the Turkish armed forces and various justice organs want," Candar wrote in the daily Sabah.
The traditional Istanbul-based business community has also backed a governing alliance that excludes Erbakan.

Whatever the exact mechanism, it appears that senior figures in the Turkish establishment -- zealous guardians of the official secular order -- played a role behind the scenes in shutting out Erbakan and his Islam-based Welfare Party.
In addition to talks with party leaders, President Demirel consulted the chief of the armed forces, the chairman of the constitutional court and the head of the intelligence service.
"There is no such thing as a 'handover'," said Yekta Gungor Ozden, head of the constitutional court, of Erbakan's doomed attempt to handpick coalition partner Ciller as his successor.
"You cannot give the task of forming a government to two people," said Ozden, putting his constitutional impramatur on Demirel's choice.

Among the Islamists, there was no doubt that pressure from the traditional elite that has ruled the republic for seven decades lay behind the president's decision. Erbakan himself denounced the move as "undemocratic."
Several pro-Welfare newspapers called the announcement the "Cankaya Coup," named for the presidential palace. The Welfare organ Milli Gazete said: "Mandate Given to the Demolition Team."
But can Yilmaz covert this impressive institutional firepower into votes in the 550-seat parliament?
His Motherland Party (ANAP) fields 129 MPs, with prospects for picking up support from the two main leftist parties, a conservative splinter group and rightist independents.
That gives him 266 seats, forcing him to rely on defections from among fellow conservatives in Ciller's DYP in order to secure a majority and win a confidence vote.

"It is 50-50 and a lot depends on the deputies in True Path," said one Western diplomat. "In the coming days Yilmaz is going to tell everyone, in particular True Path MPs, that he has the cabinet seats and other favours to give out."

Failure would give Erbakan fresh access to the corridors of power, either forcing the president to approve his power-sharing deal with Ciller or to call snap polls, which Welfare, already the biggest party, is confident it will win.

In any case, Erbakan's prospects look better than those of Ciller, now deserted by the very business and political leaders, including President Demirel, who first paved the way for her to become Turkey's first woman prime minister in 1993.

She gambled that her deal with Erbakan, backed on paper by a majority of MPs, would sway President Demirel and allow her to lead the next government. Instead, she is fighting a rear-guard action to prevent her True Path deputies from slipping away.
"When you lose power and you don't have the ministries (to dole out), well you are in trouble," said the Western diplomat. "It can be hard to get back in."

To make matters worse, the U.S.-educated Ciller faces a series of corruption cases that have so far been blocked by her Islamist partners. Formation of a Yilmaz government could mean the end of her "political immunity".
